selectedEvidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
selectedEvidence.name: Personal & Professional Development
selectedEvidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.

selectedEvidence.description2: This course describes the most widely accepted accounting theory and practice with an emphasis on using and analyzing the information in financial statements. Students learn how to comprehend a typical corporate annual report and to use accounting as a tool in understanding how economic events affect business.
selectedEvidence.name: Accounting & Corporate Finance
selectedEvidence.profile: Introduces financial accounting, management accounting and investment appraisal, including accounting's social role and accountability implications. Students record transactions, prepare and interpret financial statements, and analyze performance and financing. The course then examines costing, pricing, budgeting, organizational control and sustainable management accounting. Investment decisions are evaluated using accounting and discounted-cash-flow measures. A case study analyzes the misuse of an accounting principle and its financial-statement effects.
selectedEvidence.discipline: Financial accounting; Management accounting; Corporate finance

selectedEvidence.methods: Double-entry bookkeeping; Year-end accounting adjustments; Financial-statement preparation; Financial-ratio analysis; Variance analysis; Accounting rate of return and payback calculations; Net present value and internal rate of return; Cost-of-capital analysis; Accounting case analysis

selectedEvidence.description2: This course includes a multi-faceted exploration of AI’s business, managerial, economic and related societal implications. Designed for students with a strong interest in AI, it requires no prior technical background.
selectedEvidence.name: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
selectedEvidence.profile: Examines AI's business, economic and societal implications without requiring a technical background. AI foundations and limitations lead into applications across enterprise functions and industries, labour-market change, productivity, innovation, market structure and inequality. Governance, corporate responsibility, regulation and future scenarios connect technological developments to institutional choices. Students analyze business cases and competing scholarly arguments, then investigate a country's AI readiness, workforce, regulation and industrial policy.

selectedEvidence.description2: We study financial markets (stocks, bonds, derivatives) and financial institutions (commercial banks and central banks). We address such questions as: Can you outperform the stock market? Why are banks inherently fragile? What do central banks do? What causes financial crises? Throughout the semester, student teams participate in a business simulation, the Stanford Banking Game. Each team manages a virtual bank and tries to maximize its share price.
selectedEvidence.name: Money, Banking & Finance
selectedEvidence.profile: Examines financial markets and institutions, including the pricing of bonds, stocks and derivatives, interest rates and their risk and term structure, commercial-bank balance sheets and performance, financial structure and regulation, banking fragility and financial crises, central banks, money creation and monetary policy. Students apply algebraic and graphical analysis to financial and monetary problems. In the Stanford Banking Game they manage a simulated bank, analyse performance in Excel dashboards, forecast financial statements, and make evidence-based decisions about loans, deposits, capital, liquidity and risk. A small research project extends a selected financial or monetary research article through additional literature, a case study or updated evidence.

selectedEvidence.description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
selectedEvidence.name: Introduction to Economics
selectedEvidence.profile: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.

selectedEvidence.methods: Algebraic and graphical economic analysis; Supply-and-demand analysis; Game-theoretic analysis; IS-LM modelling

selectedEvidence.description2: Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.
selectedEvidence.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
selectedEvidence.profile: Develops microeconomic theory through consumer behaviour, imperfectly competitive markets and economy-wide allocation. Students examine choice under uncertainty, non-egoistic preferences and cognitive limitations, then monopoly, strategic behaviour and labour and capital markets. General equilibrium, efficiency, externalities and government complete the analysis. Algebraic problem-solving and graphical analysis are connected to the interpretation and evaluation of research papers.

selectedEvidence.methods: Algebraic microeconomic analysis; Graphical economic analysis; Critical evaluation of economic research

selectedEvidence.description2: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
selectedEvidence.name: Econometrics

selectedEvidence.description2: This course unpacks what drives consumer engagement with brands and how marketers build customer trust responsibly. selectedEvidence.name: Marketing & Consumer Engagement
selectedEvidence.profile: Connects marketing strategy and consumer psychology to responsible brand development and customer engagement. Students study strategic planning, customer experience, qualitative and quantitative insights, brand identity, digital marketing and behavioural framing. Applied projects analyze a company's strategy and response to disruption, design a brand, and investigate a consumer phenomenon using academic literature and primary and secondary evidence. Customer-journey mapping translates findings into recommendations.

selectedEvidence.description2: The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and social responsibilities.
selectedEvidence.name: Strategy & Digital Transformation

selectedEvidence.description2: See how companies figure out what customers love and what they don’t. You’ll plan and carry out real research, analyze what you find, and share your results. Our course shows you how to gather opinions and turn them into smart business ideas. Ready to turn curiosity into career skills? Perfect for future marketers, analysts, or entrepreneurs.
selectedEvidence.name: Market Research

selectedEvidence.description2: This course examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses. It first explores how international companies operate, then centers on key global challenges including cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade. It provides a comprehensive understanding of today’s complex international business environment.
selectedEvidence.name: International Business & Governance
selectedEvidence.profile: Examines how international trade, globalization and political, sociocultural and technological forces shape firms' cross-border decisions. Economic foundations include trade theories, foreign direct investment, foreign exchange and the monetary system. Students analyze governance, responsibility and trade-policy conflicts, investigate an international-business question, and develop an evidence-based market-entry strategy covering country attractiveness and business functions. selectedEvidence.description2: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. Entrepreneurial cases and a startup simulation examine decision-making, early growth and business lifecycles, with attention to societal impact and sustainability.

selectedEvidence.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. selectedEvidence.description2: This course offers Liberal Arts and Sciences students a deep dive into the psychological, social, and structural dynamics that shape workplaces. Through interactive case discussions, simulations, and real-world insights, students develop critical skills in motivation, leadership, group dynamics, and culture. assessment: The closest option retains all three strands: real quantitative work in calculus, linear algebra, probability, econometrics and numerical methods, implementation in programming, optimization and learning, and business questions in market research, AI adoption and accounting. The technical option replaces business applications and one algorithm course with practical C++ and Haskell development, signals and linear systems, advanced calculus and implemented reinforcement learning. The markets option replaces four computing and mathematics courses with consumer and market theory, banking simulation, market-entry study and digital strategy. Qualitative emphasis supports three different concepts beyond the numerical course differences. Market Research and Econometrics provide actual empirical work even without detailed enrichment. Linear Systems complements formal system modelling within its signal-focused scope. Neither general datasets nor course projects imply a VU-style corporate placement or a specialist logistics sequence.
repair: Repaired all three offering conflicts without changing selected codes. Kept introductory data analysis before machine learning, programming and logic before the early optimization course, and research methods before Econometrics and Leadership. Retained the mathematics prerequisite chain and documented advisory sequencing.

alignmentReview: Operations Research and Optimization Methods in AI share linear optimization and related modelling, with VU extending through integer models and network problems. Combinatorial Optimization and Advanced Algorithms share network optimization and dynamic programming. Dynamics and Computation and Linear Systems share dynamical models, with different scope in nonlinear and numerical methods. Accounting and Finance links reflect statement and valuation content, with the latter distinguished by banking and monetary scope. Revised every generic alignment explanation. Unmatched cells distinguish distributed curricular support from whole-course replacement, including projects, pipeline engineering, stochastic modelling and the capstone. Optional UCR research is extra and separate.
alignments: Both develop accounting and interpretation of financial statements. UCR also introduces costing, budgeting and investment appraisal.
Both develop financial reasoning about risk and the valuation of assets. UCR places substantial weight on banking, monetary policy and bank-management simulation.
Both develop descriptive/inferential statistical reasoning; UCR includes broad research design and group research rather than the complete VU mathematical-statistics sequence.
VU introduces the integrated discipline in a required module. UCR develops its business, mathematics and computing foundations across separate courses.
VU includes an early required analytics project. UCR has course-level research and programming projects with different aims.
VU follows its first analytics project with a second required project. UCR develops project skills across its courses.
VU requires business simulation. The UCR finance option includes a banking simulation with a narrower application.
VU requires a 12 EC company-based team case, with a joint report and product and individual assessment. UCR’s optional independent research has a separate structure.
VU reserves 30 EC for open electives. The displayed UCR plans allocate their credits to the selected themes.
Both develop set-based reasoning. UCR emphasizes logic, induction and proof, while VU also devotes study to combinatorial counting.
UCR search, constraint satisfaction and linear/nonlinear optimization overlap operations-research techniques; the full VU OR sequence remains different.
Both use dynamic programming and network optimization. UCR also studies algebraic algorithms, exact computation and measured performance.
Both develop single-variable calculus. UCR combines differentiation and integration with complex numbers and introductory differential equations.
Both teach systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear transformations. UCR connects the mathematics to applications such as least squares and principal component analysis.
Both extend the study of calculus. UCR covers multivariable methods and differential equations, with a different scope and sequence.
Both study dynamical systems; UCR focuses on linear time-invariant signals and transforms rather than the full VU dynamics/computation course.
Both study probability spaces, random variables and distributions. UCR also introduces estimation, tests and sampling simulation.
VU requires a dedicated course in stochastic modelling. UCR develops related probability and decision methods across its mathematics and AI courses.
Both teach relational database design and SQL. UCR covers normalization, authorization and query processing.
Both advance software construction beyond introductory programming. UCR uses C++ and Haskell and includes testing, version control and documentation.
Both develop supervised and unsupervised learning and model evaluation. UCR includes practical prediction and method comparison on data.
Both develop programming for computational problems. UCR uses Python and covers control flow, functions, collections, debugging and object-oriented programming.
VU Data Engineering includes building data pipelines and dashboards. UCR introduces data preparation, visualization and databases across separate courses.
VU requires a dedicated Big Data project. UCR uses datasets in several courses, with a different project structure and scale.
VU requires a dedicated Statistical Data Analysis course. UCR develops statistical practice across research methods, machine learning and econometrics.
History of Science is a separate VU requirement.
VU requires a separate Philosophy and Ethics course. The UCR courses on business AI and digital strategy address some governance and responsibility questions.
